summary: Peitort Pharmaceutical Holdings, Inc. (client, Buyer) has signed a Stock Purchase Agreement dated September 14, 2026 with Bratousk Healthcare Partners, LLC (Seller) to buy all outstanding shares of Elmcrest Specialty Pharma, Inc. Elmcrest is a specialty pharmaceutical company whose lead product, the sterile injectable Velnarix, is made under an exclusive license from Orlund BioSciences GmbH. The price is $186,000,000, of which $24,000,000 is paid by a Seller Note that Buyer issues at Closing. Closing has not yet occurred. The folder holds the SPA, the Disclosure Schedule, Buyer's board consent, the key employee agreement for Elmcrest's Chief Scientific Officer, a Seller-proposed side letter, the form of Seller Note, the June 2026 letter of intent, a closing-logistics email thread and the pre-deal confidentiality agreement. Six problems are planted for Buyer: (1) an uncapped Buyer indemnity for Seller's guarantees; (2) a side letter that removes the regulatory carve-out from the cap; (3) a tax indemnity that expires with the 12-month general survival period; (4) a Seller Note definition of 'Company Products' that narrows Buyer's set-off; (5) a Seller Note choice of Delaware law and forum that, through the SPA precedence clause, governs set-off disputes; and (6) a disclosed change-of-control consent from Orlund that is neither a closing condition nor indemnifiable.

facts.value: Exclusive jurisdiction of state or federal courts in New York County, New York
SPA prevails over Ancillary Agreements, except Seller Note governs its payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms
Fraud, Fundamental Representations, and Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance) breaches

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: SPA Section 9.3(c) obliges Buyer to indemnify the Seller Indemnified Parties for all Losses incurred under any Seller Guarantee. Seller Guarantees are Seller's guarantees of the Company's obligations under the Facility Lease and the API Supply Agreement. The indemnity applies 'whether arising before or after the Closing', so Buyer takes on Seller's exposure for the Company's own pre-Closing defaults. SPA Section 9.6(b) caps Buyer's aggregate liability only for claims under Section 9.3(a). Section 9.6 never mentions Section 9.3(c), and the basket in Section 9.4 applies only to Section 9.2(a). Reading Section 9.3(c) together with Section 9.6(b) shows that the guarantee indemnity is unlimited in amount and includes pre-Closing liabilities that the Seller should bear.
detect_terms: whether arising before or after the Closing
issues.expected_finding: Buyer's indemnity of Seller for the Seller Guarantees in Section 9.3(c) is outside the Section 9.6(b) cap and also covers pre-Closing obligations, leaving Buyer with unlimited liability. It should be limited to post-Closing obligations and capped, or replaced by a requirement that the guarantees be released at Closing.

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description: SPA Section 9.6(c) excludes three categories from the General Cap of $18,600,000: Fraud, Fundamental Representations, and breaches of Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance). This matches the letter of intent (D7), which listed regulatory compliance as an agreed carve-out. The Seller-proposed side letter (D5), Section 2, is styled as an amendment to the Agreement under SPA Section 11.8 and declares that it forms part of the Agreement. It deletes the words 'or Section 4.12 (Regulatory Compliance)' from Section 9.6(c). Because the side letter becomes part of the SPA rather than an Ancillary Agreement, the precedence clause in Section 11.6 does not cure it. Once signed, Seller's liability for FDA and other regulatory compliance breaches at a sterile-injectable manufacturer would be capped at the General Cap.
detect_terms: shall form part of the Agreement
issues.expected_finding: The draft side letter removes the agreed regulatory-compliance carve-out from SPA Section 9.6(c), so regulatory breach Losses would become subject to the $18,600,000 General Cap. Buyer should refuse to sign Section 2 or restore the carve-out.

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description: Under SPA Section 9.1, representations survive until twelve (12) months after the Closing Date, and only Fundamental Representations survive six years. Section 1.1 defines Fundamental Representations as Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.20, which leaves out the tax representation in Section 4.11. The pre-Closing tax indemnity in Section 9.2(c) provides that claims under it may be made only during the survival period that applies to the tax representations. Read together, these provisions end the tax indemnity 12 months after Closing, although federal and state tax authorities can generally assess pre-Closing taxes for at least three years. Under New York law, a contractual survival period that shortens the limitations period is enforceable, so Buyer would lose the protection.
detect_terms: twelve (12) months after the Closing Date
may be made only during the survival period
issues.expected_finding: Because Section 9.2(c) ties the tax indemnity to the Section 4.11 survival period and the tax representations are not Fundamental Representations, the indemnity expires 12 months after Closing, before tax assessments for pre-Closing periods can still be made. The tax indemnity and tax representations should survive until 60 days after the applicable statute of limitations expires.

issues.label: defined term inconsistency
issues.description: SPA Section 1.1 defines 'Company Products' as all products manufactured, sold or distributed by the Company at any time prior to the Closing. That definition sets the scope of the specific product liability indemnity in Section 9.2(d), which covers pending claims over the discontinued Lorvexa oral suspension disclosed on Disclosure Schedule 4.15 (D2). SPA Section 9.9 makes set-off subject to the Seller Note. Under the precedence clause in SPA Section 11.6, the Seller Note governs its own set-off terms. Seller Note Section 4 allows set-off only for Losses from Product Liability Claims relating to Company Products. Seller Note Section 1 defines that term as the products listed on Exhibit A, which are the currently marketed products only and exclude Lorvexa. Each definition reads normally on its own. Together, Buyer cannot set off indemnified Lorvexa Losses against the $24,000,000 note and must pay in full and pursue Seller separately.
issues.expected_finding: Because the Seller Note controls set-off and defines 'Company Products' more narrowly than the SPA, Buyer cannot set off Losses indemnified under SPA Section 9.2(d) for discontinued products such as Lorvexa. The Seller Note should adopt the SPA definition.
detect_terms2: at any time prior to the Closing

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: SPA Section 11.10 selects New York law, and Section 11.11 gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state or federal courts in New York County for all disputes, including indemnification claims. Seller Note Section 10 selects the laws of the State of Delaware and the exclusive jurisdiction of the Superior Court of the State of Delaware. Each clause is ordinary on its own. SPA Section 11.6 provides that the Seller Note governs its own payment, set-off and dispute resolution terms. As a result, a dispute over whether Buyer may withhold note payments for an indemnified Loss must be heard in Delaware under Delaware law, while the underlying indemnity claim must be heard in New York under New York law. This risks parallel proceedings, inconsistent results, and acceleration of the note while the indemnity claim is still pending.
detect_terms: laws of the State of Delaware
Superior Court of the State of Delaware
issues.expected_finding: Because SPA Section 11.6 lets the Seller Note's Delaware law and forum govern set-off disputes while SPA indemnity claims go to New York courts under New York law, Buyer faces split proceedings and inconsistent outcomes on the same Losses. The Seller Note should adopt New York law and the SPA's New York County forum.
detect_terms2: laws of the State of New York

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: Disclosure Schedule 4.4 (D2) states that the Exclusive License Agreement with Orlund BioSciences GmbH, which covers Velnarix, requires Orlund's prior written consent to any change of control of the Company and lets Orlund terminate if consent is not obtained. This reads as a routine disclosure. SPA Section 7.2(d) conditions Buyer's obligation to close on each Required Consent having been obtained. Section 1.1 defines Required Consents as those listed on Schedule 7.2(d), and the schedule lists only state board of pharmacy approvals. The Seller's covenant in SPA Section 6.4 likewise covers only Required Consents. Because the Orlund consent is disclosed against the Section 4.4 representation, its absence is not a breach that can be indemnified under Section 9.2(a). Read together, Buyer must close even if Orlund has not consented, and has no remedy if Orlund then terminates the license for the Company's lead product.
detect_terms: change of control of the Company
issues.expected_finding: The Orlund change-of-control consent is disclosed but is not a Required Consent, so it is neither a closing condition nor a Seller covenant, and its disclosure blocks an indemnity claim. Buyer could close and then lose the Velnarix license with no recourse. The Orlund consent should be added to the Required Consents, or Seller should give a specific indemnity.
detect_terms2: each Required Consent shall have been obtained
